records.name_note: This is a genus-level record, not a binomial - almost all retail moth orchids are complex interspecific hybrids with no single accepted species name. Note that Doritis and Doritaenopsis have been folded into Phalaenopsis, so older labels using those names belong here.
records.cool_rest_note: Spring-flowering large-flowered white species and hybrids need an autumn cool spell of roughly 55 F at night for about a week to initiate flower spikes. This is a bloom trigger for that group, not a general requirement, and it should not be applied to every moth orchid.
records.water_estimate_basis: Taken from NC State's stated cadence of once weekly for mature plants, more often in summer heat. It assumes the plant is mature and in the bark-based, free-draining medium the same source specifies; a plant in sphagnum or a sealed cachepot will need far less, and this figure would then drown it.
records.toxicity_detail: Clemson Extension lists moth orchids among houseplants that are safe for cats and dogs; NC State also tags the genus non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses.

records.toxicity_detail: Severity rated HIGH by NC State Extension. Leaves, stems, roots and sap all contain calcium oxalate crystals and oxalic acid. Chewing causes burning and swelling of lips, tongue and throat as needle-like crystals embed in the mouth and throat, with difficulty speaking and swallowing, and possible nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Throat swelling can compromise the airway - this warrants immediate veterinary or medical attention, and the plant is a poor choice in a home with pets or small children.
